item.title: Regardless of what it’s called, we’re clearly moving to yet another era of AI agents in our work. But as agents can both fan out and work in parallel, handle much l...
item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
Regardless of what it’s called, we’re clearly moving to yet another era of AI agents in our work.
We’ve quickly jumped from agents that spit out a quick answer for you, to today agents that you orchestrate inside of a set of tasks. But as agents can both fan out and work in parallel, handle much larger context, be able to do long running work, and have far greater levels of capabilities, we’re entering yet another level of what we can have AI do for us.
We’ll soon be able to give agents a set of goals, and they can go out and design the best solution for that goal, while also continuously improving it based on the ongoing execution of whatever it built. This will obviously start with engineering because that’s where we’re seeing the best practices emerge first in almost every new era of agents.
But the impact can be quite massive across the rest of knowledge work. You’ll tell an agent to improve your client onboarding workflow to achieve a certain targeted goal; or have agents go reduce risk in your business; or improve your security posture on an ongoing basis.
These autonomous systems will be able to take on a set of goals, design the best outcome, test and iterate, deploy, and then optimize whatever it built on an ongoing basis. Importantly, this leads to outcomes and results that humans literally couldn’t have accomplished before. This will lead to fairly new levels of productivity with AI.

Message boards were the enabling technology of both the Navier-Stokes math breakthrough and even the OpenAI/HuggingFace cyber feat.
We built a message board infrastructure primitive. You can think of it as "headless Slack" (or remember IRC?) for agents.
This is an important building block for software factories, self-optimizing systems, and scientific research, where the human prompting is just the seed of the system, and millions of agents can operate in a decentralized fashion.

But it’s hard to fathom this being sustainable. At the same time, AI Gateway token demand on Vercel has been ~40% MoM compounded since the ...
item.description:
作者：Guillermo Rauch 账号：@rauchg 简介：@vercel CEO
I’m being pitched a new inference neocloud company on average every two days. No exaggeration. I take every entrepreneur seriously and I look deeply into each.
But it’s hard to fathom this being sustainable. At the same time, AI Gateway token demand on Vercel has been ~40% MoM compounded since the beginning of the year. No signs of stopping.
One way to reconcile this is that compute is the new economy, and tokens the new energy unit. There’s a new Industrial Revolution taking place. Every aspect of our lives is being replatformed on top of this new system that enhances everything. More like an “oil rush” than a “gold rush”: it’s durable, not a fad.
In the short term, I anticipate more expansion, followed by consolidation due to economies of scale, cybersecurity and enterprise requirements (ZDR and cyber being a hot topic for inference providers), capital requirements, and an evolving regulatory landscape.

item.title: Notion’s Founder on the One Thing Your AI Is Missing
item.description:
播客：AI & I by Every
Everybody can start making their own software, no?
In some sense, the original vision of the 60s, 70s, hippie generation of computing come to life, and that's actually why Notion was started.
Notion was about how do we bring this computing power to as many people as possible without forcing them to learn how to code.
Hello and welcome to the Every Podcast.
I'm Dan Shipper.
And I'm Natalia Quintero.
And this week we're talking about a conversation that you had, Dan, with Ivan Zhao, CEO and founder of Notion.
Can you tell me a little bit about what you learned?
Yeah, it was such an interesting conversation because Notion is the original, one of the original no code companies.
The way it's structured with databases and forms and blocks, it's all designed to allow you to build something that looks kind of like software without knowing how to code.
But AI like totally changed that.
Now anyone can Vibe code whatever they want.
You don't really need a block system.
You don't really need the whole Notion interface in order to make something that looks like software.
And so it kind of forced them to reinvent what they are and reinvent or rethink the original vision for their product.
I've been a user of Notion for a long time, and the product has evolved quite a bit.
What do you think makes Ivan the right leader to lead this transformation?
You know him well.
Ivan is one of those interesting people.
I think there's some kind of soul overlap between Notion and Every, and I think that comes from who Ivan is as a person.
You know, the way that he dresses and the way that they furnish their office, and there's so much attention to detail and so much craft in what they do.
And I think that that's actually sorely missing from the...
pantheon of AI CEOs.
Like when you really think about what kinds of CEOs are around in this era, there are very few people who care a lot about the details and the feeling of work and what you make.
And especially in a world where everyone's afraid of AI taking jobs and how do you keep the work that we do feeling human or feeling special.
I think that there's something really interesting happening with Notion and Ivan is the right person to make that happen.
So if you didn't catch it at thesis, let's turn over now to a conversation between Dan Shipper and Ivan Zao from Notion.
Welcome, really excited to have you here.
Good to be here.
And thank you for sponsoring this, for making this event possible.
I didn't know until I got here.
Yeah, Ivan asked me backstage, he was like, how much was this?

It's big enough.
Good love.
Great.
Nice to be here.
So in addition to sponsoring this conference, you make Notion.
And I think of you as, we were talking about this a little bit backstage.
I think there is a spiritual similarity between the way that Notion and every think about work.
And I think that comes from you specifically.
you think a lot about the craft of work and thinking well with software.
And I think when we are, like in AI there seems like there's this bifurcation between people who think it's all slop and people who think that you can actually do good work with it.
And I'm curious like how you're thinking about this as you're bringing Notion into this era and in your own life.
We're probably in the one year after the Vibe coding phase at this point, for most people.
Probably in this room.
A year ago, people say software is dead, Vibe code everything.
Then nine months ago, people realized you need to maintain them.
I'm actually in different directions.
I love the spirit of Vibe coding.
Actually, if anything, Vibe coding, the spirit is the spirit that YNOTION was started in the first place.

Yeah.

When I was in school, last year college, I was inspired by early days of computing.
People in the 60s and 70s, or even the 50s, their idea of a software, it's a medium.
It's very much like reading and writing.
Like everybody should be able to read and write.
But if you think about it, that's actually really unnatural.
We all go through six years of school to learn how to read and write, but now we can do this.
We can write prose, we can write business report, we can write poetry.
That's not the case for computing.
That's not the case for software.

Ok this happens a lot so I thought I’ll lay it out here..
founder friend: my pitch isn’t working on the fundraising side. haaalp.
*proceeds to give me the pitch*
me: ambition is what’s being rewarded right now. what do you believe to be true if everything you laid out works? think about the second and third order effects as a result of you being successful.
founder: err, if everything works out, then “this” happens.
me: put “this” in the pitch in the first slide and walk the investor how you get to “this” by building what you’re building in the first place and how you earn the right to get there.
founder: no, they’ll think I’m crazy
me: try it. what do you have to lose?
*tries it very reluctantly*
founder (4 days later): you *insert expletive*.. it worked.
me: see. you always had it in you, you just had to tell it.
—
If you’re an ambitious founder reading this and having the same issue, try this, I think it’ll work. If it does, please tell me!!
